facts.statement: Bagualia lived during the Early Jurassic, specifically the middle Toarcian stage.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Early Jurassic (middle Toarcian), ~

facts.statement: Bagualia is an extinct genus of eusauropod dinosaur found in the Early Jurassic Cañadón Asfalto Formation of Chubut Province, Argentina.
facts.quote: Bagualia (meaning "wild horse") is an extinct genus of eusauropod dinosaur from the Early Jurassic (middle Toarcian) Cañadón Asfalto Formation in what is now the Chubut Province of Argentina.

facts.statement: The type species Bagualia alba was formally described in 2020.
facts.quote: The type species, B. alba, was formally described in 2020.

facts.statement: Bagualia is the oldest known definitive eusauropod dinosaur.
facts.quote: Bagualia represents the oldest known definitive eusauropod

facts.statement: Fossils of Bagualia were discovered in Bagual Canyon, about 4.3 km from Cerro Cóndor in Chubut, Argentina.
facts.quote: The Bagualia fossil material was discovered in Bagual Canyon, approximately 4.3 km from Cerro Cóndor in Chubut, Argentina within the Early Jurassic deposits of the Cañadón Asfalto Formation.

facts.statement: The fossils were excavated by the Museo Paleontológico Egidio Feruglio during fieldwork in 2007 and 2009.
facts.quote: The fossils were excavated by the Museo Paleontológico Egidio Feruglio during fieldwork in 2007 and 2009.

facts.statement: The fossils were found in a layer dated to around 179 million years ago that formed in a lake environment beneath a basaltic layer.
facts.quote: This layer, dated precisely to around 179 million years ago, formed in a lacustrine environment beneath a basaltic layer.

facts.statement: The fossil collection includes the holotype MPEF-PV 3301 and remains from at least three other individuals.
facts.quote: The fossils include the holotype, MPEF-PV 3301 (a partial skull with cervical vertebrae), and additional remains from at least three individuals (MPEF-PV 3305–3348).

facts.statement: The genus name Bagualia means "wild horse" in Spanish, referring to the discovery location Bagual Canyon.
facts.quote: The generic name, Bagualia comes from "bagual," the Spanish word for "wild horse," referencing the specimens' discovery in the Bagual Canyon ("Cañadón Bagual").

facts.statement: The species name alba means "dawn" in Spanish, highlighting the dinosaur's early position in the sauropod lineage.
facts.quote: The specific name, alba, is a Spanish word meaning "dawn," highlighting the dinosaur's early age in the sauropod lineage.

facts.statement: Bagualia is known from numerous bones including vertebrae, limb bones, and skull fragments from three individuals.
facts.quote: Bagualia is known from many bones from three individuals, including vertebrae from the neck, back, and tail, limb and girdle bones, as well as skull and teeth fragments.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest Bagualia's large size was aided by its digestive system and that its long neck may have helped dissipate heat like elephant ears.
facts.quote: The digestive system of Bagualia was also a likely reason why it grew to such a large size, and another function of its long neck has been proposed: it may have dissipated heat in a similar fashion to how elephants use their ears.

facts.statement: The skull of Bagualia is relatively complete.
facts.quote: The skull of Bagualia is relatively complete.

facts.statement: Bagualia possesses a unique beak-like process at the front of the upper jaw that may have supported a large keratinous structure.
facts.quote: A beak-like process is present at the anteroventral end, unique to Bagualia, which may have supported a larger keratinous structure.

facts.statement: The upper jaw of Bagualia contains 13 tooth sockets with some teeth preserved in various stages of eruption.
facts.quote: The maxilla of Bagualia shows 13 alveoli, with some teeth preserved in varying stages of eruption.

facts.statement: The lower jaw of Bagualia has 16 tooth sockets on the right side and 14 on the left side.
facts.quote: The right dentary has 16 alveoli and shows an emerging tooth, while the left dentary has 14 alveoli with five partially erupted teeth.

facts.statement: Bagualia's teeth were spoon-shaped with heavily wrinkled enamel and a forward-leaning arrangement typical of eusauropods.
facts.quote: The teeth are spoon-shaped with heavily wrinkled enamel, displaying asymmetrical mesial and distal margins, characteristic of many sauropodomorphs, with notable features like a medial convex area and a procumbent arrangement typical of eusauropods.

facts.statement: The braincase of Bagualia is nearly complete and shows a robust, tall structure similar to other eusauropods.
facts.quote: The braincase is nearly complete and ossified, showcasing a robust and tall structure similar to other eusauropods.

facts.statement: The inner ear anatomy of Bagualia shows a hypertrophied pituitary gland, which supports a link to increasing body size seen in later large sauropods.
facts.quote: In the Endocranium, pituitary gland hypertrophy supports its link to increasing body size, aligning with trends in later large-bodied sauropods.

facts.statement: Bagualia's inner ear anatomy, with shortened and widened semicircular canals, indicates reduced agility and a stable posture.
facts.quote: Its inner ear anatomy, particularly the shortened and widened semicircular canals, reflects reduced agility and a stable posture.

facts.statement: Bagualia is classified as an extinct genus of eusauropod dinosaur.
facts.quote: Bagualia (meaning "wild horse") is an extinct genus of eusauropod dinosaur

facts.statement: Bagualia is classified as an eusauropod based on features like its procumbent tooth arrangement.
facts.quote: The teeth are spoon-shaped with heavily wrinkled enamel, displaying asymmetrical mesial and distal margins, characteristic of many sauropodomorphs, with notable features like a medial convex area and a procumbent arrangement typical of eusauropods.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Bagualia's long neck functioned to dissipate heat, similar to how elephants use their ears.
facts.quote: another function of its long neck has been proposed: it may have dissipated heat in a similar fashion to how elephants use their ears.

facts.statement: Bagualia had a humerus and femur with increased eccentricity to resist bending forces in its large body.
facts.quote: The humerus and femur show increased eccentricity, reinforcing resistance to bending forces in large-bodied sauropods.

facts.statement: Features in the ulna and metacarpals indicate that Bagualia was an obligate quadruped.
facts.quote: A deep radial fossa in the ulna and changes in metacarpal proportions highlight the transition to obligate quadrupedalism.

facts.statement: Bagualia possessed a laterally projecting cnemial crest on the tibia and a wedge-shaped astragalus for refined locomotion.
facts.quote: The laterally projecting cnemial crest of the tibia and a wedge-shaped astragalus suggest refinements in locomotion.

facts.statement: All cervical vertebrae of Bagualia had an opisthocoelous structure with elongated centra and a ventral keel.
facts.quote: All cervical vertebrae exhibit an opisthocoelous structure, featuring elongated centra and a ventral keel.

facts.statement: Bagualia's proatlas was robust and rhomboid, while its atlas had elongated neurapophyses.
facts.quote: The recovered proatlas is robust and rhomboid in shape, while the atlas is distinguished by its elongated neurapophyses.

facts.statement: Features of the axis vertebra suggest the holotype of Bagualia likely belonged to a subadult individual.
facts.quote: The axis reveals notable features, such as deep lateral fossae and a prominent neural arch, indicating the holotype likely belonged to a subadult individual.

facts.statement: Bagualia's cervical ribs had a tetraradiate shape at their proximal ends with a long, slender shaft directed posteriorly.
facts.quote: Cervical ribs feature a tetraradiate shape at their proximal ends, characterized by a prominent tuberculum, capitulum, and anterior process, along with a long, slender shaft directed posteriorly, consistent with most sauropods.

facts.statement: Bagualia is classified as an early member of the group Eusauropoda.
facts.quote: Bagualia is considered to be an early member of Eusauropoda.

facts.statement: Phylogenetic analyses confirm a close relationship between Bagualia and the genera Nebulasaurus, Patagosaurus, and Spinophorosaurus.
facts.quote: Successive phylogenetic analyses from 2020, 2021, and 2024 have confirmed a close relationship between Bagualia, Nebulasaurus, Patagosaurus, and Spinophorosaurus.

facts.statement: The genus Bagualia was described by Pol et al. in 2020.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Pol et al., 2020

facts.statement: The species Bagualia alba was described by Pol et al. in 2020.
facts.quote: species_authority: Pol et al., 2020

facts.statement: The fossil remains of Bagualia consist of more than 200 bones, including axial elements, cervical vertebrae, appendicular bones, and cranial parts.
facts.quote: Los restos de Bagualia consisten en más de 200 huesos, tanto axiales como vértebras del cuello, apendiculares y craneanos.

facts.statement: Bagualia fossils come from the Cañadón Asfalto Formation in Chubut, Patagonia, Argentina, dated to 179 million years ago.
facts.quote: Su procedencia de la Formación Cañadón Asfalto, Chubut, Patagonia, Argentina, que los descriptores datan del Toarciense, 179 millones de años

facts.statement: Bagualia had broad-crowned teeth suited for tougher vegetation, unlike the thinner-crowned teeth of Patagosaurus.
facts.quote: Bagualia had broad-crowned teeth, suggesting it fed on tougher vegetation, distinct from sauropods like Patagosaurus with thinner crowns.

facts.statement: Bagualia's teeth had an enamel layer approximately 7 times thicker than other extinct herbivores, aiding in cutting conifer leaves.
facts.quote: Sus dientes están rodeados por una gruesa capa de esmalte, aproximadamente 7 veces más gruesa que la de otros herbívoros extintos, lo que permite al animal cortar mejor las hojas de las coníferas.

facts.statement: It is hypothesized that Bagualia's long neck may have functioned to dissipate heat, similar to how elephants use their ears.
facts.quote: Se ha propuesto otra función de su cuello largo, puede haber disipado el calor de manera similar a como los elefantes usan sus orejas para hacer lo mismo.

facts.statement: The holotype of Bagualia originates from the Chacritas Member of the Cañadón Asfalto Formation.
facts.quote: The holotype of Bagualia comes from the Chacritas Member of the Cañadón Asfalto Formation.

facts.statement: The depositional settings of Bagualia's habitat included tuffaceous materials, suggesting volcanic activity.
facts.quote: Both of these have intervals of tuffaceous materials, suggesting the presence of volcanic activity.

facts.statement: Bagualia lived in the "Chacritas Paleolake", a shallow, saline or hypersaline hydrologically closed lake with low-energy margins.
facts.quote: The lacustrine section has been called the "Chacritas Paleolake", and seems to have been a rather saline or even hypersaline hydrologically closed pan lake, shallow in depth, with marginal zones and palustrine subenvironments made of low-energy ramp-like margins.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Bagualia's large size was caused by a newly formed ecosystem and climate changes driven by volcanic activity in the Early Jurassic.
facts.quote: El tamaño de Bagualia probablemente fue provocado por un ecosistema recién formado y cambios climáticos, todos causados por la actividad volcánica en el hemisferio sur durante el Jurásico temprano.

facts.statement: Bagualia belongs to the parent group Eusauropoda.
facts.quote: Parent group: Eusauropoda

facts.statement: Bagualia is classified within the dinosaur class Saurischia.
facts.quote: Class: Saurischia

facts.quote: Time range: Toarcian to Toarcian (182.9 to 180.4 million years ago)

facts.quote: Fossil occurrences recorded: 1
